title: Bourbon Explained
description: A short introductory masterclass for bartenders, hospitality newcomers and anyone into whiskey: bourbon's history, how it's made and how ageing shapes its character. About 1 to 2 hours, with a certificate on completion.
topics: The legal rules that define bourbon
How bourbon became America's national spirit
Production, from grain to barrel-aged spirit
Fun facts and insider knowledge for hospitality

lessons.title: Welcome to Bourbon Explained
lessons.review:
Bourbon is America's native spirit, a whiskey made mostly from corn and aged in new charred oak. In 1964 the US Congress recognised it as a distinctive product of the United States.

It is sweeter and rounder than most Scotch, with vanilla, caramel and toasted oak from those new barrels.

This course covers where bourbon came from, how it differs from other whiskies, the mash bill, the legal definition, ageing, and what proof really means.

questions.explain: Corn makes up the majority of the mash.
Bourbon can be made anywhere in the USA.

questions.q: Typical bourbon flavours from new charred oak?
questions.explain: New charred oak gives vanilla, caramel and toast.

lessons.title: The history of bourbon and American whiskey
lessons.review:
Settlers in Kentucky and Pennsylvania distilled their surplus grain in the late 1700s. A federal tax on whiskey sparked the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794, pushing many distillers further west.

The name is linked to Bourbon County in Kentucky and to Bourbon Street in New Orleans, where the spirit was shipped and sold.

Prohibition (1920–1933) shut most distilleries. The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 had earlier set the first quality guarantee for American whiskey.

questions.q: What sparked the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794?
questions.explain: Farmer-distillers rebelled against the whiskey tax.
Prohibition lasted from 1920 to 1933.
It set rules guaranteeing authentic, aged whiskey.

lessons.title: How bourbon is made differently to whisky
lessons.review:
Most bourbon starts in a column still, often followed by a "doubler" or "thumper", rather than the pot stills of single malt.

Many distillers use the sour mash process: some spent mash from the last run is added to the new fermentation to keep it consistent.

Bourbon must go into new charred oak containers. Scotch, by contrast, often matures in casks that held bourbon, sherry or wine before.

questions.q: What does the sour mash process do?
options: Reuses some spent mash to keep fermentation consistent
questions.explain: Backset from the last run keeps conditions steady.
New, charred oak is required by law.

questions.q: Where do many used bourbon barrels go?
options: To Scotch and other whisky makers
questions.explain: Used bourbon barrels are widely reused for Scotch and more.

lessons.title: What is a mash bill?
lessons.review:
The mash bill is the grain recipe. By law, bourbon must be at least 51% corn, and most use around 60–80%.

The rest is usually malted barley (for its enzymes) plus a flavouring grain: rye for spice, or wheat for a softer, rounder "wheated" bourbon.

High-rye bourbons taste peppery and bold; wheated bourbons are gentler and sweeter. The mash bill is the first clue to a bourbon's style.

questions.explain: At least 51% corn is required.
Rye brings a peppery spice.
Wheat gives a gentler profile.

lessons.title: How bourbon is defined
lessons.review:
To be called bourbon it must be made in the USA from at least 51% corn and aged in new charred oak containers.

It must be distilled to no more than 80% ABV (160 proof), go into the barrel at no more than 62.5% ABV (125 proof), and be bottled at 40% ABV (80 proof) or more.

Nothing can be added except water. Straight bourbon is aged at least two years, and if it is under four years old the label must state its age.

questions.q: Can colouring or flavouring be added to bourbon?
questions.explain: Only water may be added.
At least 80 proof.

questions.q: Straight bourbon is aged at least?
questions.explain: Straight bourbon needs two years or more.

lessons.title: How bourbon is aged and why
lessons.review:
Barrels are charred inside; the heaviest level is known as "alligator char" for its cracked look. The char filters the spirit and unlocks caramelised sugars in the wood.

In Kentucky's hot summers and cold winters the spirit pushes into the wood and is drawn back out, picking up colour and flavour. All of bourbon's colour comes from the barrel.

Barrels sit in warehouses called rickhouses, and where a barrel sits (top floors are hotter) changes how fast it matures.

questions.q: Where does bourbon get its colour?
questions.explain: All colour comes from the barrel.

options: Temperature swings move spirit in and out of the wood
questions.explain: Heat and cold drive spirit into the wood and back.
Rickhouses store maturing barrels.

lessons.title: What do proof and ABV mean?
lessons.review:
ABV, alcohol by volume, is the percentage of the liquid that is alcohol. It is the measure used on Australian labels.

In the US, proof is simply double the ABV: 40% ABV is 80 proof, 50% ABV is 100 proof.

"Bottled in Bond" whiskey is bottled at exactly 100 proof, while "barrel proof" or "cask strength" is bottled at the strength it came out of the barrel.

questions.q: A bourbon at 45% ABV is how many US proof?
questions.explain: Proof is double the ABV.
Bonded whiskey is exactly 100 proof.

options: Bottled at the strength from the barrel
questions.explain: No dilution before bottling.
